# Frequently asked questions

Questions that often come up after this lecture, with short answers. Click to open.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## How much data do I need to train a neural network?

It depends on the number of inputs and on how complicated the function is, but as an order of
magnitude: hundreds of samples for a smooth function of 2–3 inputs, thousands to hundreds of
thousands for tens of inputs or images. The honest way to know is a **learning curve**: train on
10 %, 30 %, 100 % of your data and look at the test error. If it still decreases, more data will
help. In exercise 1 you will see the surrogate degrade with 50 samples instead of 2400.
If you have only 10–100 points, prefer a Gaussian process or a physics model with a few fitted
parameters.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Why not simply use the physics simulation directly?

You should, whenever it is fast enough and accurate enough! ML is useful when (a) the simulation
is too slow for the task (an optimisation needing 10⁵ evaluations, an online model at 10 Hz),
or (b) the simulation does not match the real machine and data must fill the gap. A good
surrogate is always validated *against* the simulation.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## How do I choose the number of layers and neurons?

There is no formula. Start small (2–3 hidden layers of 32–64 neurons), check training and
validation errors, and increase the size only if the model underfits (both errors high). If it
overfits (validation error much higher than training error), get more data, reduce the size or
add regularisation. These choices are called **hyper-parameters** and are tuned on the
validation set — never on the test set.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Is the gradient descent guaranteed to find the best solution?

No. It finds a *local* minimum, the bottom of the valley where it starts (slide "the same idea in
two dimensions"). For neural networks this is surprisingly not a big problem in practice: with
many parameters, most local minima are about as good as each other. For tuning a machine it can
be: restart from several points, or use a global method such as Bayesian optimisation.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## What is the difference between a Gaussian process and a neural network?

Both are flexible regression models. A **Gaussian process** gives a prediction *and* an
uncertainty, works very well with few data (10–1000 points) and few inputs (≲ 20), but its cost
grows like $N^3$ with the number of points. A **neural network** gives no uncertainty by default,
needs more data, but scales to millions of points, many inputs and images, and is very fast once
trained. Rule of thumb: few expensive points → GP; many cheap points → NN.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Why "Bayesian" optimisation?

Because the Gaussian process is a Bayesian model: it starts from a *prior* belief on the function
(smooth, with a certain length scale) and updates it into a *posterior* after each measurement
using Bayes' rule. The uncertainty band you see is the spread of this posterior.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Can we trust an ML model in the control room?

Only within limits you control. Good practice: the model acts through the usual control system,
actuator changes are bounded and ramped, an operator can stop it, and the previous settings can
be restored in one click. Monitor the model's inputs: if they leave the training range, the
predictions are not reliable. Methods that give uncertainties (GPs, ensembles of networks) help
detect this.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Reinforcement learning or Bayesian optimisation?

Bayesian optimisation needs no training and works out of the box, but each tuning takes tens of
evaluations and it does not "remember" between runs. A reinforcement-learning agent needs a long
training (in simulation) but then tunes in a few steps and can act as a feedback. At ARES (DESY)
both were compared on the same task (Kaiser *et al.*, Sci. Rep. 2024). Start with BO; consider
RL when the same task is repeated very often and a good simulator exists.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## What is the advantage of a differentiable simulation like Cheetah?

It gives the derivative of any output with respect to any input in one extra pass, with no
finite differences. With 100 magnets, finite differences need 100+ simulations per gradient;
automatic differentiation needs about 2. This makes gradient-based tuning, model calibration
and the training of neural networks or RL agents coupled to the simulator much faster. Cheetah
is also fast in itself, which is why it is used to train RL agents.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Do I need a GPU?

Not for this course nor for most accelerator applications with tabular data: everything in the
exercises runs on a laptop CPU in seconds to minutes. GPUs matter for large networks, images and
large-scale RL training. Google Colab offers a free GPU if you need one.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Where is ML used today in accelerator operation?

Bayesian optimisation is used routinely for tuning at several facilities (e.g. FEL pulse energy
at LCLS, injector tuning at many labs, often via Xopt). Anomaly detection of BPMs has been used at
the LHC, fault classification of SRF cavities at CEBAF, virtual diagnostics at LCLS/FACET-II, and
RL has been demonstrated on real machines at CERN (AWAKE, LINAC4) and DESY (ARES). The references
are on the [resources page](resources.qmd).
:::

# Self-check quiz

Try to answer before opening the solution.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. What are the four ingredients of (almost) every ML method?

Data, a model with adjustable parameters, a loss measuring how wrong the model is, and an
optimiser that changes the parameters to reduce the loss.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. The training loss diverges (grows to huge values) after a few steps. What is the first thing to try?

Reduce the learning rate: the steps overshoot the minimum.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. A neuron has weights $w = (1, -2)$, bias $b = 0.5$ and ReLU activation. What is its output for the input $(2, 1)$? And for $(0, 1)$?

$z = 1\cdot2 - 2\cdot1 + 0.5 = 0.5$ → output $0.5$.
For $(0, 1)$: $z = -2 + 0.5 = -1.5$ → output $0$ (the neuron is "off").
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. How many parameters (weights + biases) has a network 2 → 10 → 1?

Hidden layer: $2 \times 10 + 10 = 30$. Output: $10 \times 1 + 1 = 11$. Total **41**.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 5. Why is a randomly split test set often too optimistic on accelerator data?

Consecutive shots are correlated and the machine drifts, so randomly chosen test samples are
almost copies of training samples. Test on data from another run or another day.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 6. In Bayesian optimisation, why is the next point sometimes chosen far from the current best?

Because the acquisition function also rewards *uncertainty* (exploration): a region with no
measurements might hide a better optimum.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 7. You have 10 years of archived BPM data and nobody has labelled the faults. Which family of methods?

Unsupervised anomaly detection (PCA reconstruction error, Isolation Forest, autoencoders).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 8. Why does a reinforcement-learning agent usually train in simulation first?

It needs $10^4$–$10^6$ episodes, far too many for beam time; and random actions at the start could
be unsafe on a real machine. It is then transferred to the machine (sim-to-real).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 9. A surrogate is very accurate on the test set but wrong on the machine. Name two possible reasons.

(a) The machine settings are outside the training range (extrapolation). (b) The simulation used
for training does not describe the machine (magnet errors, misalignments, drifts). Also possible:
different units or calibrations between simulation and control system.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 10. What does `loss.backward()` compute in Cheetah/PyTorch?

The derivatives of the loss with respect to every trainable parameter (e.g. the quadrupole
strengths declared as `nn.Parameter`), by automatic differentiation — the chain rule applied
through the whole beamline.
:::
